paragraphs.text: Old paper gives off hundreds of compounds as it ages. Together they produce the sweet, slightly sour smell that many readers like, and which no perfume has copied exactly.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Conservators use the smell as a tool. A portable device samples the air around a book and reports which compounds are present, which tells them how fast the paper is breaking down.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The method is gentle: nothing is cut from the page, and the book need not leave the shelf. Older tests required a small piece of paper, which libraries were reluctant to give.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Results are not always easy to read. A book stored next to a window gives different figures from the same edition kept in a cool room, so conservators record where each copy has been.
paragraphs.label: D

items.prompt: an advantage over earlier methods of testing
a factor that makes the figures harder to compare
a description of the equipment used
